pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 6–7 (UK Y2, US Grade 2–3). Solving multiplication and division PROBLEMS using arrays, repeated addition, mental methods and known facts — the application layer that ties the early representations to real contexts.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'solve problems involving multiplication and division, using materials, arrays, repeated addition, mental methods, and multiplication and division facts, including problems in contexts'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.OA.4 (array totals via equal addends) building toward 3.OA.3 'use multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems in situations involving equal groups, arrays, and measurement quantities'.
• Operational details: the goal is to CHOOSE and use an efficient representation for a given problem — an array, repeated addition, a jump on a number line, or a recalled fact — and to recognise whether a story is multiplication or division. Push from counting-all toward using known facts.
• Checkpoint: model and solve in context. Tier A (6): solve a simple equal-groups problem with an array or repeated addition. Tier B (6–7): choose a sensible representation and solve both a grouping and a sharing story. Tier C (7): solve using a known fact rather than counting all, and explain why that's quicker.
bestPractices: Give real, contextual problems (equal groups, arrays, simple sharing) and let children choose the representation — array, repeated addition, number-line jumps, or a known fact — rather than prescribing one method.
Explicitly move children from 'count everything in ones' toward 'use a fact or a group structure', highlighting the efficiency gain so they are motivated to leave counting-all behind.
Include both multiplication and division stories (and both division structures) so problem-recognition — deciding which operation a story needs — is practised, not just computation.
Use the bar model and array to represent the structure of a word problem before calculating, so meaning drives the method.
Connect back to known 2, 5, 10 facts so problem solving rehearses and applies fluency rather than relying on re-counting.
keyRepresentations: Known multiplication/division facts applied to context
commonMisconceptions: Counting every object in ones instead of using groups or a known fact — not progressing in efficiency.
Not recognising which operation a word problem needs (multiplication vs division; sharing vs grouping).
Modelling with unequal groups and still treating it as multiplication.
Grabbing the numbers and operating without representing the problem's structure first.
Muddling the roles of the numbers (number of groups vs group size) when setting up the calculation.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7 (UK Y2, US Grade 2–3): solving multiplication and division word problems by CHOOSING and using an efficient representation — an array, repeated addition, number-line jumps, or a recalled fact — and recognising whether a story calls for multiplication (combining equal groups) or division (splitting into equal parts), and within division whether it is sharing or grouping. The developmental goal is to move children from counting everything in ones toward using group structure or known facts, and to represent a problem's structure before calculating.

activities.title: Problem playground: model the story, then solve
feedback: If a child writes 5 + 2 = 7 for '5 bags of 2', act out the five groups with objects, count the total, and connect it to 2+2+2+2+2 and 5×2 so the groups-of structure is felt.

If a child shares 15 among 3 but ends with unequal piles or a miscount, model round-robin 'one for each' dealing and check at the end that the piles are equal — the sharing idea is there, the execution needs tightening.
If an array for 4 × 3 is ragged or has the wrong count, align rows and columns neatly, count rows × per-row, and connect the tidy array back to the numbers 4 and 3.
Correct answers to anchor on: 5 bags of 2 = 10 apples (2+2+2+2+2, or the fact 5×2); 15 shared among 3 = 5 each; 15 in bags of 3 = 5 bags; a 4-by-3 array totals 12.
activities.rationale: Choosing and applying a method across both multiplication and division stories (including both division structures) practises problem-recognition, not just computation, and keeps meaning ahead of calculation. Manipulable modelling lets children see whether their representation matches the story.
sourceClaims: Y2: solve problems involving multiplication and division using materials, arrays, repeated addition, mental methods and facts, including problems in contexts.
3.OA.3 use multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems involving equal groups, arrays and measurement quantities.
learnerActions: Read a contextual equal-groups or sharing story (e.g. '5 bags with 2 apples in each — how many altogether?').
First decide: is this a multiplication story (combining equal groups) or a division story (splitting into equal parts — by sharing or by grouping)? State your choice before solving.
Choose how to model it: build an array, lay equal jumps on a number line, write it as repeated addition, or use a known fact.
Solve and check that your model actually matches the story (equal groups, the right group size and number of groups).

Repeat with a sharing story (e.g. 'Share 15 sweets equally among 3 children'), a grouping story (e.g. '15 sweets are put into bags of 3 — how many bags?') and an array task (e.g. 'Draw an array for 4 × 3').
activities.intendedInsight: A word problem's structure (equal groups, array, or sharing/grouping) determines which operation and representation fit; meaning should drive the method rather than grabbing the numbers and operating blindly.

activities.title: Count-all vs known fact: the efficiency race
feedback: If a child still counts every object, point out the time/effort difference they just saw and prompt: 'Which fact could land this answer straight away?'
Check that both methods reach the same total. If they agree, that agreement confirms the fact. If they differ, recount, because counting in ones can go wrong too.
Keep any demo total tied to a fact the child actually knows — e.g. if 24 is used, link it to the 2-times fact 2×12, or choose a 5- or 10-fact — so the recall step is genuinely available to them.
activities.rationale: Explicitly highlighting the efficiency gain motivates the shift from counting-all toward using facts — the developmental move this topic exists to produce. A side-by-side comparison makes the gain concrete; the demonstration shows relative speed rather than a proven intervention.
sourceClaims: Y2: solve problems involving multiplication and division using materials, arrays, repeated addition, mental methods and facts, including problems in contexts.
learnerActions: Take one problem whose total comes from a fact the child knows (e.g. 2×12 = 24, a 2-times fact) and solve it two ways: once by counting every object in ones, and once by using the recalled fact.
Watch the counting-all method work slowly up to the total while the known fact lands the answer at once.
Say why the fact is quicker, and try the next problem using a fact instead of counting all.
activities.intendedInsight: For a child who knows the fact, recalling it (or using group structure) is much quicker than counting everything in ones — this efficiency gain is the motivation to leave counting-all behind.

activities.title: Is it × or ÷? Sort and match the stories
feedback: If a story is matched to a wrong-operation sentence, return to acting out the situation to decide whether numbers are combined into equal groups or split into equal parts.
Praise reasoning that cites the story's structure ('there are equal groups, so it's multiplication') rather than guessing from the numbers.
activities.rationale: Matching stories to operations and spotting wrong-operation distractors rehearses and checks problem-recognition. This format exercises operation/method choice but does not itself elicit building a model, so pair it with hands-on modelling.
sourceClaims: Y2: solve problems involving multiplication and division using materials, arrays, repeated addition, mental methods and facts, including problems in contexts.
learnerActions: Read several everyday stories and sort each one: is it a multiplication (combining equal groups) or a division (splitting into equal parts) situation? For each division story, also say whether it is sharing (number of groups known) or grouping (group size known).
Match each story to the number sentence that fits it (e.g. an equal-groups story to 5 × 2, a sharing story to 15 ÷ 3).
For a tricky pair, explain what in the story tells you which operation to use.
Watch for distractors that combine the two numbers with the wrong operation (e.g. 5 + 2 or 15 − 3).
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising which operation a word problem needs — and, within division, whether it is sharing or grouping — is a distinct skill from doing the arithmetic.

activities.title: Market-stall problems: talk through your method
feedback: If a child names a method without justifying it, ask them to point to what in the story makes that method fit.
Follow a spoken plan by actually building or jotting the model, so the reasoning is tied to a concrete representation.
activities.rationale: Prompting children to reason aloud about method choice supports problem-recognition and metacognition. Spoken reasoning elicits articulation and justification but does not itself produce a built model or the side-by-side speed comparison, so pair discussion with hands-on modelling and with the count-all vs known-fact comparison to ground the efficiency insight.
learnerActions: A character (e.g. a market-stall seller) poses an everyday equal-groups buying problem and asks 'how would you work it out?'
Say aloud which operation and representation you would use and why.
Try a follow-up that changes the numbers (e.g. 'If there were 6 bags of 2, how many apples then?') and explain how your method adapts.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to articulate and justify a chosen strategy deepens understanding of why a representation fits a problem.

constraints: Include both multiplication and division stories, and both division structures (sharing and grouping), so problem-recognition is practised — not just computation.
Represent the problem's structure (array, bar model, or number line) before calculating, so meaning drives the method.
Connect back to known 2, 5, 10 facts so problem solving rehearses and applies fluency rather than relying on re-counting; keep any demonstrated fact within the facts the child actually knows.
Let children choose the representation rather than prescribing one method.
Matching/multiple-choice sorting rehearses and checks problem-recognition but does not by itself teach how to construct a model; pair it with hands-on modelling.

A fixed illustrated worked example (tap-to-reveal array and fact) can show one case but cannot provide the varied, decision-rich practice of choosing and applying a method; use it as a scaffold, not the main task.
These problems are modelled with flat arrays, bars and number lines; a 3D presentation is not expected to add conceptual value for this topic — a design judgement here, not a general rule.
Keep the bar model/array as a tool for the structure of the word problem, not as decoration added after the answer.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original 'race to 24' moment is retained as a motivating device; '24' is illustrative, not tied to the worked examples (which total 10, 5 each, and 12). Any concrete total used should match a fact the child actually knows (e.g. 24 = 2×12, a 2-times fact).
The second cited source (CCSS 3.OA.3) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its support as unconfirmed.

The 'efficiency race' and the framing that counting-all is slower are pedagogically motivating but not empirically established comparative efficacy; presented as a demonstration of relative speed, not a proven intervention.
Note 2.OA.4 (array totals via equal addends) was mentioned in the pedagogy as a building-block standard but is not in the row's sources[] list; it is not cited as a sourceClaim.

'Grouping' is treated as one of the two division structures (quotitive), distinct from the equal-groups structure of multiplication; the binary × vs ÷ sorts were reworded to avoid mislabelling multiplication as 'grouping'.

probeDeeper: Which of these is a sharing problem and which is a groups problem?
Could you use a times-table fact instead of drawing it all?
If there were 6 bags of 2, how many apples then?
assess.correctAnswer: 10 apples (5 groups of 2, or 2+2+2+2+2, or the known fact 5×2); 5 each (15 shared into 3 groups); a 4-by-3 array totalling 12 — choosing a fitting representation and reaching the right total.

errorPatterns.pattern: operation confusion — for '5 bags of 2' writes 5 + 2 = 7, combining the numbers rather than making equal groups
errorPatterns.nextMove: act out the groups with objects, count the total, and connect it to 2+2+2+2+2 and 5×2 so the groups-of structure is felt
errorPatterns.revealedBy: adds or subtracts the two numbers instead of grouping

errorPatterns.pattern: shares unequally or loses track — deals 15 among 3 but ends with unequal piles or miscounts
errorPatterns.nextMove: model round-robin dealing 'one for each' and check the piles are equal at the end — the sharing idea is there, the execution needs tightening
errorPatterns.revealedBy: unequal shares or a wrong count in the sharing task

errorPatterns.pattern: array mismatched to the factors — draws 4 × 3 as a ragged or wrong-count arrangement
errorPatterns.nextMove: align the rows and columns neatly and count rows × per-row; connect the tidy array back to the numbers
errorPatterns.revealedBy: array rows/columns don't line up with 4 and 3

responseLevels.gap: Combines the two numbers with the wrong operation, or cannot represent the situation at all.
responseLevels.full: Chooses a fitting strategy for both grouping and sharing problems, represents each accurately (array / repeated addition / known fact), and reaches correct totals.
responseLevels.partial: Solves the equal-groups problem but is unreliable on sharing, or reaches answers only by drawing every object with no move toward known facts.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Solve these, and show your working with objects, an array, or a jotting. (1) There are 5 bags with 2 apples in each — how many apples altogether? (2) Share 15 sweets equally among 3 children — how many each? (3) Draw an array to work out 4 × 3. (Watch which strategy they choose and whether it fits the problem.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The multiplication and the division sit side by side, so the task reveals whether the child selects the right structure (grouping/repeated addition versus sharing) and can represent it. A struggling child adds or subtracts the two numbers (5+2, 15−3), builds groups of the wrong size, or draws an array that doesn't match the factors. Watching the working — not the answer alone — shows whether the strategy is sound.
